q: Lecture 15 – Retina – slide 12: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Preproliferative diabetic retinopathy

  • (1) intraretinal microvascular anomalies (vascular bypasses);
  • (2) ischemic retinal infarcts with cotton wool spots or soft white-greysh exudates;
  • extensive areas where capillary bed is closed (capillary nonperfusion zones) leading to retinal anoxia and hypoxia;
  • (3) severe macular edema.

q: Lecture 15 – Retina – slide 13: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (retinitis proliferans)

  • neovascularization
  • new vessel formation on the retina or optic disk
  • prone to leakage
  • bleeding repeatedly into the vitreous.
  • preretinal and vitreous hemorrhages
  • eventually associated with fibro-glial proliferation infiltrating the vitreous structure.
  • irregular shrinkage pulls away the retina resulting in traction retinal detachment.

q: Lecture 15 – Retina – slide 14: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (retinitis proliferans)

  • sight strongly depressed
  • the angiogenesal factor (VEGF) produced by hypoxic retina may pass into the anterior segment
  • rubeosis iridis and neovascular glaucoma

q: Lecture 15 – Retina – slide 16: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Treatment

  • proliferative diabetic retinopathy
  • panretinal photocoagulation
  • destroying the peripheral retina
  • exception of the central retinal zone.
  • the principle of converting hypoxic areas of capillary closure to anoxic scars by photocoagulation
  • widely applied in proliferative diabetic retinopathy,
  • particularly when neovascularization of the optic disk is well developed.
  • antiangiogenezal agents
  • bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept
  • vitrectomy
  • advanced proliferative retinopathy.

q: Lecture 15 – Retina – slide 18: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Retinitis pigmentosa

  • Signs
  • retinal arteries are attenuated,
  • papilla is yellow
  • waxy pale aspect
  • dendritic black pigmented cells
  • bone corpuscle shaped clumps of pigment in the mid periphery of the retina.
  • absence of the electroretinogramm
  • earliest signs.

q: Lecture 15 – Retina – slide 26: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Diagnostic considerations and findings:

  • Central retinal vein occlusion
  • linear or punctiform hemorrhages in all four quadrants of the retina
  • distended and increasingly meandering veins.
  • branch retinal vein occlusion,
  • intraretinal hemorrhages in the area of vascular supply;
  • one quadrant or in two quadrants (hemispheric vein occlusion).

q: Lecture 15 – Retina – slide 30: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Branch retinal artery occlusion,

  • retinal edema in the affected area of vascular supply
  • Perimetry
  • total visual field defect in central retinal artery occlusion
  • partial defect in branch occlusion.

q: Lecture 15 – Retina – slide 32: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Retinoblastoma

  • Treatment
  • large tumors,
  • enucleation
  • small and middle size tumors
  • radiotherapy with episcleral plaque of iodine or cobalt
  • an alternative to enucleation
  • should perforate the eyeball
  • exenteration of the orbit
